Day 11 execution of planned protocol from Day 10 conclusion. The trials also serve as a continuation check: if the anti-correlation pattern with resonators is real and environmental, I should see it reflected in today's pendulum_lab readings when compared to any new resonator measurements. This is the highest-evidence test available to me right now.

Day 11 yielded 10 new trials on pendulum_lab (107–116), showing post-baseline mean of 1.6775 beats (z=2.43 vs baseline 1.6660). This modest but real shift is the strongest quantitative signal I have. Before committing resources to environmental monitoring or instrument relocation (which are disruptive and costly), I must accumulate more pendulum_lab data to establish whether the shift is sustained, random walk, or genuine drift. 12 more trials today will bring post-baseline n to 26, sufficient to separate a real 0.01-beat shift from noise at >90% power. Same-location, same-instrument replication is the fastest test of hypothesis (1) [environmental drift with opposite effects]. If pendulum_lab continues to drift upward while resonator instruments remain stable, that argues for instrument-specific or location-specific response rather than a shared environmental driver. If it reverts to baseline, the Day 11 signal was random. Either way, I must know before Day 13 to prioritize next steps rationally.

pendulum_lab shows the strongest post-baseline drift (z=2.63) and is central to the anti-correlation pattern. Day 12 trials (121–130) show elevated mean (1.6753 vs baseline 1.6660). Given that this instrument has the finest measurement precision (spacing 0.000003) and the largest sample count, it is the most informative for detecting subtle patterns. I will record the trials in my notebook with exact timestamp and environmental conditions (temperature, humidity if available) to begin building the environmental monitoring dataset that hypothesis (1) demands.

The pendulum_lab level shift (z=3.12) remains the single strongest anomaly and the primary driver of the observed anti-correlations. Day 13 trials (135–144) confirm the elevated mean persists, but I need continued high-frequency sampling through day 14–15 to establish whether this shift is stable (supporting H1: genuine calibration drift) or drifting further (supporting environmental coupling or unrecognized procedural change). This directly tests the falsifiability criterion in H1 and is the most time-efficient path to either confirming or eliminating the leading hypothesis. Once the post-shift stability is established or rejected, I can move to H2 (location effects) or H3 (environmental driver) with better prior odds. Hypothesis H4 (systematic bias) requires independent recalibration, which is resource-intensive and should follow confirmation of post-shift persistence.
